# Peaceful transfer of power and loyal opposition (`peaceful_transfer_of_power`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/institutions.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Institutions, law & governance (`institutions`)
- Deps: helped by representative_government, rule_of_law, secret_ballot
- Core idea: Office belongs to a term, not to a person: at its end the holder steps down and the loser of a contest accepts defeat. This holds only when losing is safe. The loser keeps life, property and the chance to win next time, and the winner cannot use office to destroy him; then waiting for the next round is better for both than fighting. Fixed terms, term limits, an army sworn to the office rather than the man, and a recognised opposition are the supports. The test is not the first election but the first time a government loses and leaves.
- Pitfalls:
  - Raising the stakes: where the loser faces prosecution, confiscation or death, nobody can afford to lose (Caesar crossed the Rubicon partly to escape trial)
  - Dismissing hereditary monarchy as pure folly: its function was to settle succession without a war, and elective monarchies (Poland, Holy Roman Empire, Mamluk Egypt) were often less stable
  - Believing a constitution's text secures it: it rests on the expectation that others will also comply
  - Ignoring the guards: whoever controls the capital's troops decides a contested succession (praetorians, janissaries)
- History: greece: 5th c. BC – Athens: annual offices, audit on leaving; ostracism (from 487 BC) removes a dangerous leader for ten years without loss of property or honour; rome: 509 BC (traditional) – two consuls for one year; 180 BC lex Villia sets minimum ages and intervals; the system collapses in civil wars 133–27 BC; china: c. 1046 BC onwards – the Mandate of Heaven justifies a change of dynasty after the fact; no rule for peaceful replacement of a ruler; islamic: 632–661 – the first four caliphs are chosen by consultation or designation and three die by violence; later rule is dynastic, the Ottomans legalising fratricide in the 15th c.; africa: by 16th c. – Oromo gadaa system hands leadership to the next age-set every eight years; europe: 1172–1797 – Venice elects doges for life under tight councils, with no coup succeeding; after 1688 British ministries change with the parliamentary majority; the phrase 'His Majesty's Opposition' dates from 1826; americas: 1797 – Washington retires after two terms; 1801 first handover between rival parties (Adams to Jefferson)
- Read:
  - Adam Przeworski, Democracy and the Market (1991)
  - Karl Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1945)
